A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAW research work. Their complete 33-page contents, including Appendices A–J and the checklist, are readable; text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable judgments.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulated-control results for SAW and implemented comparison methods, including benchmark evaluations, waypoint-advantage diagnostics, ablations, and stitching experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results in Section 6 and Appendices H–J, including Tables 1 and 3 and Figures 3–8.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the SAW objective in Equation 9, value learning, target-subpolicy training, and inference procedure are unchanged. The added stability discussion introduces no method component.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 20 main state- and pixel-based OGBench datasets and the additional stitch/explore evaluations in Appendix J. No task, domain, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 retain GCBC, GCIVL, GCIQL, QRL, CRL, HIQL, and offline RIS. Comparator membership also remains unchanged in the subgoal-representation experiments and GCWAE diagnostics.

E3.justification: The five-goal evaluation, binary success-rate metric, goal-sampling distributions, architectures, and hyperparameters remain unchanged in Section 6 and Appendices F–G. No new experimental protocol is introduced.

E4.justification: The subgoal-representation tests in Figure 3, waypoint-advantage diagnostics in Appendix H, and one-step AWR and temperature ablations in Appendix I are unchanged. No analysis tests the newly proposed variance-reduction explanation.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across eight seeds, with four seeds for visual tasks, using the same table captions and uncertainty displays. The new discussion of training variance adds no statistical estimation or uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Success-rate entries in Tables 1 and 3, curves in Figures 3–8, and reported experimental findings are unchanged. Rendered comparisons confirm that the result displays are identical.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, and derivations in Section 5 and Appendices A–B are unchanged. Edits to equation punctuation and wording about approximate posteriors do not revise the mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central claims remain a flat policy without a subgoal generator, a common derivation connecting SAW with HIQL and RIS, and strong long-horizon performance. Removing a repeated closing passage does not remove these claims, which remain elsewhere.

C2.justification: Section 8 newly hypothesizes that stable subpolicy action targets reduce the gradient variance associated with noisy advantage weights, connecting this explanation to Section 4.3. This is explicitly speculative; the existing sampling-bias and stitching limitations remain unchanged in Section 7.

D1.justification: Hardware and runtime disclosures, implementation details, and hyperparameters in Appendices E–G are unchanged. The project-page link and statements about code access also remain the same.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning relative to hierarchical RL, RIS, and planning invariance are unchanged. Reference 10 gains the journal name Neural Computation, which is a bibliographic metadata correction.

P1.justification: Section 8 is partially rewritten, with the chunking analogy reframed as an addendum. There are scattered grammar, terminology, and punctuation edits, plus updated author information and reference metadata; section and appendix organization remains unchanged.

P2.justification: The title page replaces the shared author block with separate author/affiliation blocks, and the revised Discussion locally reflows. All figures, tables, captions, legends, and their placements remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2’s closing recap, v3 offers a more informative, explicitly qualified explanation connecting stable subpolicy targets to possible variance reduction. Small wording and presentation corrections also improve clarity. The gain is limited: the experiments and derivations are unchanged, so the proposed mechanism remains untested.
